     BLACK JACK RANCH TRUST, AND HARKEY RANCH ENTERPRISES, INC.

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

       Pursuant to SOAH Order No. 32 issued in this docket, John D. Harkey, Jr., The Mason
Trust, Black Jack Ranch Trust, and Harkey Ranch Enterprises, Inc. (together, “Harkey Ranch”)
timely file this Reply Brief and respectfully shows as follows:

                                       I.      INTRODUCTION

       Harkey ranch respectfully submits this Reply brief in further support of Route 894, the
route selected by Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC ("Oncor") and LCRA Transmission
Service Corporation ("LCRA") (collectively, “Applicants”) as the route that best meets the
applicable routing criteria under the Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) 1 and the Public
Utility Commission of Texas’ (“PUCT” or “Commission”) Substantive Rules. Alternatively,
Harkey Ranch does not oppose Route 487, as recommended by Commission Staff, or any route or
modification which includes Links K42 or L1. Harkey Ranch strongly opposes Route Cherokee
Creek G ("CCG"), Route 572, as well as any route or route modification that includes either Link
L1 or Link K42.



       1
           TEX. UTIL. CODE §§ 11.001-66.016.


Harkey Ranch’s Initial Brief
SOAH 473-26-16349 || PUC 59475                                                        Page 1 of 9
        The Initial Briefs filed by parties advocating Route CCG and 572 do not overcome the
comparative route evidence demonstrating that Route 894 best balances the applicable routing
criteria. Instead, they deflect from the clear, holistic picture provided by that data and attempt to
elevate a subset of the routing data as dispositive. Specifically, this Brief is intended to reply to
those Initial Briefs filed by Route CCG and 572 advocates Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors
and Segment K13/K51 Landowners.

        The comparative route evidence confirms why Route 894 is preferable to Route CCG and
Route 572: compared to Route 894, CCG is approximately 9.02 miles longer, approximately
$73.69 million more expensive, has 20 more habitable structures within 500 feet, has 55 more
stream crossings, has more potential wetlands, has more recorded cultural resources within 1,000
feet, has more high archeological/historical site potential, and crosses 24 more FM/county/street
roads.2 Against Route 894, Route 572 is approximately 2.52 miles longer, approximately $8.33
million more expensive, has 22 more habitable structures within 500 feet, has 45 more stream
crossings, has more high archeological/historical site potential, crosses more FM/county/street
roads, has less compatible ROW paralleling.3 Route 894 avoids K42 and L1 while better aligning
with the Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance among the routes of interest and while also
recording no park crossing, no park within 1,000 feet, and no park foreground-visual-zone length.4
The evidentiary record correctly reflects the governing principle: route selection requires a
reasoned balancing of all factors and is not a mathematical exercise.5 That principle supports the
selection of Route 894, not Route CCG or Route 572.

       For the reasons discussed herein, Harkey Ranch respectfully requests that the Honorable
SOAH ALJs recommend, and the Commission approve, selection of Route 894 or another
alternative route that does not utilize links L1 and K42.

                                               II.      ARGUMENT

   A. Route 894 remains the route that best satisfies the routing criteria set forth in PURA
      and in Commission rules.
       Applicants’ Initial Brief confirms that Applicants identified Route 894 as the route that
best meets the applicable routing factors.6 Applicants also explained that routing requires a
reasoned balancing of all relevant factors, including the factors addressed in PURA § 37.056(c)(4)
and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), and that the weight assigned to any factor may vary based on the
facts and circumstances of the case.7 That is precisely the approach Harkey Ranch supports.

       Route 894 performs well across the measurable routing criteria prescribed under PURA
and Commission rule. It is not the lowest-cost Route of Interest, but it is lower in cost than Route
CCG and Route 572.8 It is not the shortest route of interest, but it is shorter than Route CCG and
Route 572.9 In their Initial Brief, Applicants assert that each of the routes proposed in their
Application and by parties to this proceeding are reasonably comparable to each other based on
estimated cost and habitable structures identified within 500 feet of each route.10 Harkey Ranch
respectfully disagrees with that assertion. Notably, Route 894 has only 85 habitable structures
within 500 feet of the centerline - the fewest among the Routes of Interest.11 It also crosses no park
or recreational area, has no park or recreational area within 1,000 feet, and has no ROW within the
foreground visual zone of any park or recreational area.12

       Commission Staff witness John Poole, while recommending Route 487, testified that he
considers Route 894 to be “a very good route.”13 Mr. Poole also acknowledged that Route 894 has
20 fewer habitable structures than Route CCG, that Route CCG is much longer than Route 894,
and that Route CCG’s additional length results in more cost.14 Applicants’ panel similarly testified

agreed on Route 894 as the route that best meets the routing criteria required to be considered.15

        The comparative routing data, as included in the table below for ease of reference, for
Route 894, Route CCG, and Route 572 demonstrate why Route 894 is preferable:16

Referencing the data above, Route CCG’s only notable advantage over Route 894 in this limited
comparison is additional compatible ROW paralleling. Route CCG achieves that marginal
advantage by adding approximately nine miles of transmission line, 20 habitable structures, 55
stream crossings, and increasing cost by approximately $73.69 million. Route 572 cannot claim
that same slim advantage because Route 572 has less compatible ROW paralleling than Route 894
while still adding length, cost, habitable structures, 45 more stream crossings, high
archeological/historical site potential, road crossings.

    B. The record does not demonstrate meaningful route superiority for Routes CCG or
       572.

        i.         Community Values, Prudent Avoidance, Habitable Structures

        Intervenors advocating for Routes CCG or 572 do not establish meaningful route
superiority over Route 894 that would justify the substantially greater impacts and costs associated
with those alternatives. Rather than demonstrating a superior overall balance of the applicable

 routing criteria, supporters of those proposed routes principally seek to shift impacts away from
particular intervenors. Those intervenors contend in their Initial Briefs that the significant habitable
structure difference between Route 894 and Route CCG should be discounted because it falls
within a standard deviation or quartile band ranking.17 Such statistical standards have not been
adopted by the Commission as standard routing methodology and should not be allowed to
transform meaningful differences in assessed routing criteria.18 Route 894 best serves community
values and adheres to the Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance because it minimizes direct
residential exposure. Route 894 has only 85 habitable structures within 500 feet of the route
centerline, which is the fewest of the eight Routes of Interest.19 By comparison, Route 894 includes
20 fewer habitable structures than Route CCG, and 22 fewer than Route 572.20 Selecting Route
CCG or Route 572 would result in a 24% and 25% increase in affected habitable structures,
respectively. That increase is not reasonably comparable to Route 894, and it’s difficult to see that
increase seeming reasonably comparable to affected homeowners. Route 894 also moderates
impacts on landowners by keeping cost and length comparatively low, and maintaining meaningful
use of compatible rights-of-way and property boundary paralleling.21

      ii.          Cost

       The Commission’s rule expressly requires consideration of cost.22 Applicants explain in
their Initial Brief that the transmission line cost estimates for the filed routes were developed using
a rigorous and uniform methodology and provide a reliable apples-to-apples basis for comparing
routes.23 Applicants further explain that the same methodology was applied uniformly to the links
and routes, so differences among the estimates reflect route-specific construction requirements and
provide a reliable basis for distinguishing among routes.24 Route CCG costs approximately $73.69
million more than Route 894, and Route 572 costs approximately $8.33 million more than Route

 894.25 Of the 122 routes Applicants filed with their Application, only 15 of those routes have a
total estimated cost greater than Route CCG.26 $74 million dollars more in cost is simply not
reasonably comparable in comparison to Route 894, and it would be difficult to imagine residential
customers viewing this significant extra cost as inconsequential. Those are significant differences
that, when balanced holistically with the applicable routing criteria, are not outweighed by
selective emphasis on certain criteria.

      iii.         Recreational and Park Areas

        The comparative routing data show that Route 894 crosses no park or recreational area, has
no park or recreational area within 1,000 feet, and has zero miles within the park foreground visual
zone.27 Routes CCG and 572 share those results, but they do not uniquely achieve them nor do the
results distinguish Routes CCG and 572 from other routes that perform better on balance, as Route
894 does. Route CCG and Route 572 supporters emphasized park viewshed in briefing.28 However
testimony from Ms. Reinecke on this topic undercuts that emphasis. Ms. Reinecke admitted that
she had not visited Link J31 and had not visited the location where any segment of the line would
run.29 She also said she assumed, not knew, that Post Oak Ridge State Park could still be seen from
Link J31.30

      iv.          Environmental Integrity

        Harkey Ranch does not dismiss the importance of Colorado Bend State Park, Post Oak
Ridge State Park, the Colorado River, the San Saba River, or the Hill Country resources discussed
by other parties through briefing and in the evidentiary record. Those resources are important. But
advocates for Routes CCG and 572 seek to make those concerns dispositive, while minimizing the
comparative routing data, contrary to the holistic analysis required by PURA and the
Commission’s rules.

           Proponents of Route CCG likewise emphasize river crossings at the Colorado and San Saba
Rivers.31 Comparing Routes 894, CCG, and 572, Routes CCG and 572 have significantly more
stream crossings – Route CCG with 55 more, and Route 572 with 45 more.32 Route CCG
proponents likewise emphasize that Route CCG crosses the Colorado River near an existing
pipeline corridor and crosses the San Saba River near an existing transmission line. 33 But Route
894’s Colorado River crossing was selected through Applicants’ holistic routing process, and the
Applicants’ panel testified that, when looking at that feature, Route 894’s Link J22 was favorable
for the crossing, parks, and related considerations over Route CCG’s Link J31.34 Moreover, Route
CCG’s San Saba River crossing next to an existing transmission line may carry its own risk.
Mr. Poole, for Commission Staff acknowledged that locating the proposed transmission line next
to an existing AEP line at the San Saba River crossing creates the risk that an event damaging both
lines could create a potential single point of failure.35

          On balance, the record developed in this matter shows that Route 894 best addresses and
satisfies the applicable routing criteria.

    C. Any route selected should exclude Links L1 and K2.

          Among the Routes of Interest, only Routes 572 and CCG include Link K42, and none of
them include Link L1.36 Multiple feasible routes therefore avoid both links while performing as
well as or better than the routes that include Link K42 as to cost, habitable structures,
cultural/historical metrics, and stream crossings.37 Route 894 is the strongest of those and avoids
both Link L1 and Link K42 while outperforming the Routes of Interest that include Link K42, as
discussed herein.
          Link K42 alone or in combination with Link L1 would threaten safe aircraft operations at

 the Ranch's two runways and nearby residences. It would place a large transmission-line obstacle
complex in a location that materially interferes with safe use of the Ranch runways. Selection of a
route including both Link K42 and Link L1 creates a deadly right angle or box canyon hazard.38
At the Hearing on the Merits, Harkey Ranch stipulated on the record that with regard to those
hazards, Randal Langford, Harkey Ranch’s witness on aviation safety, agrees that they would be
reduced if Link L4 was substituted for Link L1 and that those concerns would be eliminated if
neither Link L4 nor Link 1 are used.39 Harkey Ranch further stipulated that Mr. Langford believes
Link K42 would pose a danger and would prefer it not be chose, he agrees that the use of Link
K42 alone would be preferable compared to the use of Link K42 in conjunction with either Link
L4 or L1.40 This confirms that the aviation safety concerns posed by inclusion of Links L1 or K42
can be reduced but would still remain a serious safety concern.
       Link L1 would materially impair headquarters and agricultural infrastructure, irreparably
harm historical, aesthetic, geological, and ecological resources, and impose avoidable easement
and damage costs where less harmful and less expensive routing options exist.41 Therefore, routes
avoiding Link L1 and Link K42 should be preferred.42
       The Commission should not require Texans to bear severe, avoidable impacts to their land
and property when, under the applicable routing criteria, there is a more efficient and less harmful
route. Route 894 satisfies the Project need, remains viable and constructible, and best balances the
statutory and Commission rule criteria while avoiding or significantly diminishing such
detrimental impacts. Harkey Ranch does not oppose the Project; however, given the profoundly
destructive impact that the Project would have if sited along or within the Harkey Ranch, any
selected route should therefore exclude Link K42 and Link L1.

                                              III.   CONCLUSION

       For the reasons stated above, Harkey Ranch respectfully requests that the Administrative
Law Judges recommend, and the Commission approve, selection of Route 894 for the Project.
